# Electric-Magnetic Duality in Linearized Gravity with a Cosmological Constant

## Overview

This paper investigates the implementation of electric-magnetic duality transformations in the context of four-dimensional gravity. Specifically, we consider the theory linearized around maximally symmetric backgrounds, namely Minkowski space and (anti-)de Sitter space, (A)dS₄. Electric-magnetic duality, a symmetry principle with deep roots in gauge theory and gravitation, provides a powerful framework for understanding the structure of these linearized theories and reveals subtle features that emerge when a cosmological constant is present.

## The Role of the Cosmological Constant

A central result of our analysis concerns the interplay between duality transformations and the presence of a cosmological constant. In flat space, duality can be implemented cleanly at the level of the canonical formalism. However, once a non-vanishing cosmological constant is introduced, the situation changes qualitatively: duality transformations generically modify the Hamiltonian of the system. This means that the generator of time evolution is not left invariant under the duality map, marking an important distinction between the flat-space and (A)dS cases.

## Invariance of the Bulk Dynamics

Remarkably, despite the fact that the Hamiltonian is altered by the duality transformation, the underlying bulk dynamics of the theory remains unchanged. In other words, the physical equations of motion and their solutions in the bulk are preserved under duality, even though the canonical description is reorganized. This demonstrates that the modification of the Hamiltonian does not signal a change in the physical content of the theory, but rather reflects a redistribution of the canonical structure that leaves the local dynamics intact.

## Boundary Terms and Their Origin

The reconciliation of these two facts—the modified Hamiltonian on one hand, and the invariant bulk dynamics on the other—lies in the boundary terms generated by the duality transformations. We devote particular attention to the careful identification and analysis of these boundary contributions. The discrepancy in the Hamiltonian is entirely accounted for by terms localized at the boundary, which become physically significant precisely because of the asymptotic structure of (A)dS spacetimes.

## Implications for Holography

Finally, we discuss in detail the consequences of these boundary terms for holography. Because boundary data play a fundamental role in the holographic description of gravitational theories in asymptotically (A)dS backgrounds, the boundary terms generated by duality carry direct physical meaning for the dual boundary theory. We explore how these terms influence the holographic dictionary and what they reveal about the action of electric-magnetic duality on boundary observables, thereby connecting the canonical analysis of duality to broader questions in the holographic correspondence.

# Electric-Magnetic Duality in Linearized Four-Dimensional Gravity

## Introduction

Electric-magnetic duality has long served as a powerful organizing principle in theoretical physics, relating seemingly distinct descriptions of the same underlying physical system. Originally understood in the context of Maxwell's electromagnetism—where the source-free equations exhibit a symmetry under the interchange of electric and magnetic fields—this concept has been extended to a wide variety of field theories, including linearized gravity. In this work, we examine electric-magnetic duality transformations in four-dimensional gravity linearized around maximally symmetric backgrounds, namely Minkowski space and (anti-)de Sitter space (AdS₄ and dS₄). Our particular focus is on the boundary terms that these duality transformations generate, which have often been overlooked but prove to be of substantial physical importance.

## Duality in the Presence of a Cosmological Constant

When gravity is linearized around a flat Minkowski background, the graviton shares many formal properties with the photon, and the duality transformation acts cleanly on the phase space of the theory. The situation becomes considerably more subtle, however, once a nonzero cosmological constant is introduced, corresponding to linearization around an (A)dS₄ background.

The presence of a cosmological constant has an important consequence: the duality transformation generically modifies the Hamiltonian of the theory. In other words, the generator of time evolution is not invariant under the exchange of electric and magnetic degrees of freedom. This might initially suggest that duality fails to be a genuine symmetry of the system. Crucially, however, this is not the case at the level of the dynamics. Despite the transformation of the Hamiltonian, the **bulk equations of motion remain unchanged**—the physical evolution of the gravitational field in the interior of the spacetime is preserved. The duality thus continues to relate physically equivalent configurations, even though its action on the canonical structure is nontrivial.

## The Role of Boundary Terms

The resolution of this apparent tension lies in a careful treatment of boundary terms. When one performs the duality transformation, the modification of the Hamiltonian manifests itself precisely through the generation of surface terms localized at the boundary of the spacetime. These boundary contributions must be handled with care, as they are responsible for the difference between the transformed and original Hamiltonians while leaving the bulk dynamics intact.

Far from being mere technical artifacts, these boundary terms carry genuine physical content. In a theory with well-defined asymptotic behavior—as is required for a consistent variational principle and for the definition of conserved charges such as energy and angular momentum—the boundary terms determine the global properties of the system. Understanding how duality acts on these terms is therefore essential for a complete characterization of the symmetry.

## Implications for Holography

The significance of these boundary terms becomes especially pronounced in the context of holography. In the AdS/CFT correspondence, the asymptotic boundary of anti-de Sitter space is where the dual conformal field theory is understood to reside, and boundary data in the bulk gravitational theory translates directly into physical quantities in the boundary theory. Consequently, the boundary terms generated by the duality transformation have direct implications for the holographically dual description.

In particular, the way duality reshuffles boundary conditions and surface charges can correspond to nontrivial operations in the dual field theory, potentially relating different boundary theories or different sectors of the same theory. The interplay between electric-magnetic duality and holographic boundary conditions thus provides a valuable window into how bulk symmetries are encoded on the boundary, and into the broader structure of the gauge/gravity correspondence.

## Conclusion

In summary, our analysis demonstrates that electric-magnetic duality in linearized four-dimensional gravity remains a symmetry of the bulk dynamics even in the presence of a cosmological constant, despite the fact that it modifies the Hamiltonian. The careful accounting of the boundary terms generated by the transformation not only clarifies the status of the duality but also reveals connections to holographic physics that merit further investigation.

# Minkowski and Hamiltonian: Foundations of Modern Physics

## Introduction

The concepts of Minkowski spacetime and the Hamiltonian formulation represent two cornerstones of theoretical physics. While they emerged from different mathematical traditions—one from geometry and relativity, the other from classical mechanics—both have become essential tools for understanding the physical universe.

## Minkowski Spacetime

Named after the German mathematician Hermann Minkowski, Minkowski spacetime provides the geometric framework for Einstein's special theory of relativity. In 1908, Minkowski recognized that space and time should not be treated as separate entities but rather as unified into a single four-dimensional continuum.

The key innovation was the introduction of a spacetime interval that remains invariant across different reference frames:

$$ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2$$

This mathematical structure captures the essence of relativity: while different observers may disagree about measurements of time and distance, they all agree on this fundamental interval. The famous statement by Minkowski—"Henceforth space by itself, and time by itself, are doomed to fade away into mere shadows"—elegantly summarizes this revolutionary perspective.

## The Hamiltonian Formulation

The Hamiltonian, developed by Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton in the 19th century, offers a powerful reformulation of classical mechanics. Rather than describing systems through forces and accelerations, the Hamiltonian approach focuses on energy.

The Hamiltonian function, typically denoted **H**, represents the total energy of a system expressed in terms of positions and momenta:

$$H = T + V$$

where T represents kinetic energy and V represents potential energy. The evolution of a system is governed by Hamilton's equations:

$$\dot{q} = \frac{\partial H}{\partial p}, \quad \dot{p} = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial q}$$

## The Connection in Modern Physics

The true power of these concepts emerges when they combine in advanced physics. In quantum field theory and relativistic quantum mechanics, physicists must reconcile the Hamiltonian formulation with the requirements of Minkowski spacetime.

This synthesis presents challenges. The Hamiltonian naturally singles out time as special—it generates time evolution—while Minkowski spacetime treats time on equal footing with spatial dimensions. Resolving this tension has led to profound developments, including the Lagrangian formulation of field theory, which preserves manifest relativistic invariance.

## Conclusion

Together, Minkowski spacetime and the Hamiltonian formulation illustrate the deep interconnection between geometry, energy, and dynamics. Their continued relevance across classical mechanics, relativity, and quantum theory testifies to the enduring power of mathematical insight in revealing the structure of physical reality.

Extending this analysis to (Anti-)de Sitter backgrounds, we demonstrate that the cosmological constant obstructs a naive duality rotation at the level of the equations of motion, since the mass-like curvature terms break the symmetry between the dual field strengths. We show, however, that duality can be restored by suitably combining the linearized Weyl tensor with the background curvature, and we clarify the role of the (A)dS radius as a deformation parameter that interpolates continuously to the flat-space result. The dual formulation is related to the original one by a canonical transformation, ensuring equivalence of the physical spectrum while realizing the duality symmetry non-locally in the potentials.

# Electric-Magnetic Duality in Linearized Gravity: Boundary Terms and Holographic Implications

## Abstract

We investigate the implementation of electric-magnetic duality transformations in four-dimensional linearized gravity, with particular attention to the role of boundary terms and their holographic interpretation. Building on the structural analogy between linearized general relativity and Maxwell theory, we formulate the gravitational duality rotation that interchanges the electric and magnetic components of the linearized Weyl tensor while preserving the Fierz-Pauli equations of motion. We demonstrate that this duality constitutes a symmetry of the free graviton action, but that its consistent realization requires careful treatment of the double-dual curvature tensor and the introduction of a suitable prepotential formulation.

Working within the Hamiltonian framework, we show that the graviton phase space admits two symmetric transverse-traceless tensor potentials whose canonical structure renders the SO(2) duality invariance manifest at the level of the action. We derive the associated conserved current and analyze the surface integrals that arise when spacetime possesses a boundary, showing that non-trivial boundary terms must be added to preserve duality covariance and to ensure a well-defined variational principle. These boundary contributions are shown to modify the symplectic structure and to encode the asymptotic charges of the theory.

In the holographic context, we examine the imprint of gravitational duality on the boundary of asymptotically anti-de Sitter and asymptotically flat spacetimes. We establish that the electric-magnetic duality of the bulk graviton corresponds to a transformation exchanging the boundary stress tensor with a dual response function, providing a gravitational analogue of the S-duality relating Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions. We discuss the connection between these dual boundary data and the linearized versions of the holographic Weyl anomaly and boundary gravitational currents. Our results clarify the interplay between bulk duality symmetries, boundary dynamics, and the conserved charges relevant to the asymptotic symmetry algebra, offering insight into the extension of electric-magnetic duality beyond the free theory and its potential significance for a holographic understanding of gravitational degrees of freedom.

---

*Keywords:* electric-magnetic duality, linearized gravity, Weyl tensor, boundary terms, holography, asymptotic charges, prepotential formalism
